title: Open Match: Overview and Step-by-Step Introduction

blocks.t: Open Match experience: overview and step-by-step introduction Argentics Follow 6 min read · Jan 5, 2023 2
Today we will share an article from Argentic’s CTO, Yulian. He will introduce you to Open Match, an open-source matchmaking framework based on Kubernetes.

Why do you need Open Match? “First, I need to explain the challenges many developers face with matchmaking services. Matchmaking is one of the hardest unsolved problems for online multiplayer games. At a fundamental level, matchmaking takes players to connect to your games, match them up and connect them to game servers. Creating a good match is critical to your game’s success. You must consider attributes like skills, level, latency, wait time, and others. All those parameters are critical to your game. Making a good matchmaking service for your game is hard, but it’s core logic related to your game design. Running this on a global scale for your player population presents a whole different set of challenges. Architecting a matchmaking service that can run at high skill reliably is very hard and may not be an interesting problem for a game developer. This is exactly why Open Match was created.

So Open Match is an open-source matchmaking framework co-founded with Unity. It leverages Kubernetes to provide flexibility, scalability, and extensibility. To give you an example of the scale it can handle, maybe you remember the Halloween Doodle from 2018, that 4v4 multiplayer game you could play from the Google.com website. Halloween Doodle by Google integrating Open Match Yeah, that one was using Open Match to match players. And it handled a concurrent peak of 500,000 players. Because, with Open Match, you don’t need to worry about the scalability and reliability of the underlying infrastructure; you can focus on building the core logic of your matchmaker. Because I think a picture is worth a thousand words, let’s take a look at the high-level architecture of how online games will integrate with Open Match.

You have a game front end with your core game logic on the left side. That calls into the matchmaking framework. And at the same time, on the right side, you have a pool of servers that players can be placed on that’s simultaneously calling in the matchmaking logic. Open Match sits in the middle, handling available players, splitting them by skill level, latency, etc., and matching them up with available servers. As a developer, you only care about developing the match function, which contains the core logic of your matchmaker. The left and right boxes are components from your game that you need to integrate with Open Match. Let’s take a closer look at those components in the left and right boxes. The game front end is the endpoint to which your game clans will connect. To avoid cheating, you don’t want them to directly connect to the Open Match front end because only your game front end can verify the game clans’ data by accessing a database containing the player’s data.

So basically, your game front end creates matchmaking requests called Tickets in Open Match. You find the game back end, also called Director and the dedicated game servers on the right side. Your game back end is a key component in the matchmaker since it triggers the match function execution. Once Open Match finds matches, it will also handle the game service assignment to the match players. You can reuse this architecture across your games as you build multiple games. Match step by step For a better idea of the match, let’s take a look at the life of a match step by step. In the first step, a player wants to play against other players. The game clan requests your game front end to find a match.

The game front end makes the request to the Open Match front end to find a match. Every request is stored in the state store running on Redis. As I mentioned, the game back end triggers the match function using the Open Match back end. The game back end requests for a match. The Open Match back triggers the matchmaking function that uses the query component to create Redis and find candidates for a match. Once a match is found, the Open Match back end will return it to the game, finalizing the matchmaking process by assigning a dedicated game server to the match players. The last step of the life of a match is the assignment. It’s the last step, where we assign a game server to the matched players. For the game back end, we allocate a dedicated game server by using solutions like Agones or any other custom server management system. Once it gets the allocated game server IP and port, it will reach out again to the Open Match back end to update the tickets stored in the state store with that information. Finally, once tickets have been updated, the game front end will push the game server details to players, who will then connect to the server and start to play. And, voila, that’s how Open Match works in a nutshell. Hope this was clear enough.”

If you’re building a small game, you might not be interested in a complex, highly-scalable matchmaking framework. But you can still leverage Open Match to write a simple matchmaking function that will look like a single function in the language of your choice. Plug that into the framework, and you’ll have a fully functional matchmaking service without much work. But where Open Match really shines is if you have a really large system with thousands or millions of players that are all coming at the same time. And the player population is segmented into different groups and matched up very quickly. You might be running hundreds of concurrent matches on the player population, looking for the best match to make your game work. Case Soon we will share how our game dev studio used Open Match in our latest Desktop game, “Try Hards.”

“Try Hards” is a free-to-play and top-down 3D action game for Desktops where two teams with up to 5 members in each could fight one against the other. You control a character called a Fanatic. In general, we implemented 20 different characters separated between 4 races. Now our game is available in all European countries and the USA. In one of the next articles, we will describe how matchmaking in Try Hards works. Follow for more!
